title: Junction Transistor
short_intro: A junction transistor is a three-terminal semiconductor device formed by sandwiching either a thin layer of p-type semiconductor between two n-type layers (n-p-n) or an n-type layer between two p-type layers (p-n-p). It functions primarily as a current-controlled amplifier or a solid-state switch.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Working principle of n-p-n and p-n-p transistors, biasing conditions for active, cut-off, and saturation regions, transistor current components (I_E = I_B + I_C), and common-base (CB) and common-emitter (CE) current gains (α and β).
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Detailed mathematical analysis of common-collector configuration, hybrid equivalent parameters (h-parameters), thermal runaway, stability factor, DC load line analysis, and transistor biasing circuits (voltage divider bias).

prerequisites: Energy bands in solids and Fermi level
p-n junction diode forward and reverse biasing characteristics
Minority and majority charge carrier dynamics in semiconductors

concept_notes.heading: Structural Regions of a Transistor
bullets: The Emitter is heavily doped to supply a large number of majority charge carriers into the base region.
The Base is extremely thin and lightly doped to minimize the recombination of injected charge carriers before they reach the collector.
The Collector is moderately doped and physically larger than the emitter and base to effectively dissipate heat generated by collecting charge carriers.

concept_notes.heading: Transistor Biasing and Operating Regions
bullets: Active Region: Emitter-base junction is forward-biased and collector-base junction is reverse-biased; used for linear amplification.
Saturation Region: Both emitter-base and collector-base junctions are forward-biased; the transistor acts as a closed switch.
Cut-off Region: Both emitter-base and collector-base junctions are reverse-biased; the transistor acts as an open switch.

concept_notes.heading: Current Components in a Transistor
bullets: The total emitter current (I_E) is the sum of hole and electron currents crossing the emitter-base junction.
A small fraction of carriers recombine in the base, constituting the base current (I_B).
The remaining major portion of injected carriers crosses into the collector, constituting the collector current (I_C).

concept_notes.heading: Transistor Configurations
bullets: Common-Base (CB) Configuration: Base is common to input (emitter) and output (collector); characterized by low input impedance, high output impedance, and voltage gain with current gain (α) less than unity.

Common-Emitter (CE) Configuration: Emitter is common to input (base) and output (collector); characterized by moderate input impedance, moderate output impedance, and high current gain (β) greater than unity.

Common-Collector (CC) Configuration: Collector is common to input (base) and output (emitter); characterized by very high input impedance, very low output impedance, and voltage gain close to unity (voltage follower).

derivations.title: Relation between Common-Base Current Gain (α) and Common-Emitter Current Gain (β)
derivations.conditions: Active region operation with negligible reverse saturation leakage current (I_CBO)
steps: Write the fundamental current relation for any transistor: I_E = I_B + I_C.
Define the common-base current gain as α = \Delta I_C / \Delta I_E \approx I_C / I_E.
Define the common-emitter current gain as β = \Delta I_C / \Delta I_B \approx I_C / I_B.
Substitute I_B = I_E - I_C into the definition of β: \beta = \frac{I_C}{I_E - I_C}.
Divide numerator and denominator by I_E: \beta = \frac{I_C / I_E}{1 - (I_C / I_E)}.
Substitute I_C / I_E = α into the expression to yield the final relation.

derivations.title: Relation including Collector-to-Base Leakage Current (I_CEO)
derivations.conditions: CE configuration accounting for minority carrier reverse saturation current
steps: Start with the fundamental CB collector current equation: I_C = \alpha I_E + I_CBO.
Substitute I_E = I_B + I_C into the collector current equation: I_C = \alpha (I_B + I_C) + I_CBO.
Rearrange terms to collect I_C on the left side: I_C (1 - \alpha) = \alpha I_B + I_CBO.

graphs_and_experiments.title: CB Input Characteristics
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Curves of input current (I_E) versus input voltage (V_EB) for various constant values of output voltage (V_CB).
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Resemble forward-biased p-n junction diode characteristics. A change in V_CB has a negligible effect on the curves.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Evaluates understanding of input resistance determination (r_e = \Delta V_EB / \Delta I_E at constant V_CB).

graphs_and_experiments.title: CE Output Characteristics
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Curves of collector current (I_C) versus collector-emitter voltage (V_CE) for different constant base currents (I_B).
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Shows three regions: active (nearly horizontal flat curves), saturation (steep rise at low V_CE), and cut-off (I_C \approx 0 when I_B = 0).
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Frequently tested for identifying operating regions, load line plotting, and determining output resistance.

graphs_and_experiments.title: DC Load Line and Q-Point
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A straight load line equation I_C = -\frac{1}{R_L} V_CE + \frac{V_CC}{R_L} superimposed on the CE output characteristics intersecting the active region at the Quiescent point (Q).
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: The Q-point defines the DC operating voltages and currents without any signal input. Proper placement ensures distortion-free amplification.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Numerical and conceptual questions on maximum signal handling capacity and thermal stability.

solved_numericals.question: In a transistor, the collector current is 2.4 mA and the base current is 0.1 mA. Find the emitter current and the current amplification factor α.
solution_steps: Use the fundamental current relation: I_E = I_B + I_C.
Substitute the given values: I_E = 0.1 \text{ mA} + 2.4 \text{ mA} = 2.5 \text{ mA}.
Calculate the current gain β = I_C / I_B = 2.4 / 0.1 = 24.
Calculate α using the relation α = \beta / (1 + \beta) or α = I_C / I_E = 2.4 / 2.5.

solved_numericals.question: The common-base current gain α of a transistor is 0.98. What is the change in collector current if the emitter current changes by 2 mA?
solution_steps: Recall the definition of common-base current gain: α = \Delta I_C / \Delta I_E.
Rearrange the formula to solve for the change in collector current: \Delta I_C = \alpha \times \Delta I_E.
Substitute the given values: \Delta I_C = 0.98 \times 2 \text{ mA}.

solved_numericals.question: A transistor connected in common-emitter mode has a current gain β = 50. The load resistance R_L is 4 kΩ, and the internal input resistance is 500 \Omega. Calculate the voltage gain and power gain of the amplifier.
solution_steps: Use the formula for voltage gain in CE mode: A_v = \beta \times (R_L / r_{in}).
Calculate power gain using A_p = \beta \times A_v: A_p = 50 \times 400 = 20000.

assumptions_and_limitations: Junction transistors operate under low-frequency small-signal approximations unless high-frequency hybrid-π models are employed.
Carrier recombination in the base is assumed constant, though it varies slightly with temperature and operating voltage.
Transistor parameters are treated as linear over small excursions around the operating point.

common_misconceptions.wrong: The collector current is greater than the emitter current because the collector is larger.
common_misconceptions.correct: The emitter current is always the largest current in a transistor (I_E = I_B + I_C).
common_misconceptions.why: The emitter supplies all carriers; some are lost in the base, so collector current must be strictly less than emitter current.

common_misconceptions.wrong: A transistor can step up power passively without an external DC power supply.
common_misconceptions.correct: Amplification is a process of transferring a signal from a low-resistance circuit to a high-resistance circuit using DC source energy.
common_misconceptions.why: Conservation of energy holds; power gain is achieved by drawing DC power from the bias batteries.

common_misconceptions.wrong: The base region of a transistor should be heavily doped to facilitate current flow.
common_misconceptions.correct: The base region is extremely lightly doped and very thin.
common_misconceptions.why: Light doping and small thickness minimize electron-hole recombination in the base, ensuring high collector current.

quick_revision: I_E = I_B + I_C always holds true irrespective of configuration.
Alpha (α) is always less than 1, whereas beta (β) is typically between 20 and 500.
Active region requires EB junction forward-biased and CB junction reverse-biased.
